runs: It had looked perfect in the fridge: a tall golden pillar flecked with rosemary, a little cotton wick standing proudly in the middle. I carried it to the table inside a hollowed sourdough loaf, lit it, and stepped back to enjoy the gasps. They came, briefly. Then the candle leaned. Then it slumped. The rosemary around the wick began to smoke, and within ten minutes my showpiece looked like a melted snowman in a bread bowl. Everyone was very kind about it. I was mortified.

runs: So I did what home cooks do. I went back to the kitchen and started taking notes. I learned that butter straight from the store behaves very differently from butter that has been softened to the right temperature. I learned that herbs and cheese packed right up against a wick are what cause sputtering and smoke, and that a simple column of clarified butter around the wick fixes it completely. I learned which molds release cleanly, how long a candle really needs to chill, how warm a room can be before a candle starts to lean, and which wicks belong anywhere near food (and which never do).

runs: Almost every failed edible candle fails for one of five reasons. Once you know them, they are easy to avoid, and every recipe in this book is built to avoid them.
items.html: Almost every failed edible candle fails for one of five reasons. Once you know them, they are easy to avoid, and every recipe in this book is built to avoid them.
items.text: Almost every failed edible candle fails for one of five reasons. Once you know them, they are easy to avoid, and every recipe in this book is built to avoid them.

runs: The butter was the wrong temperature.

Butter that is too cold won't pack, so it traps air pockets that later cause cracks and collapses. Butter that is too warm turns greasy, separates and never sets cleanly. The fix: soften butter to 65 to 68°F (18 to 20°C). It should hold a fingerprint without looking shiny.

Butter that is too warm turns greasy, separates and never sets cleanly. The fix: soften butter to 65 to 68°F (18 to 20°C). It should hold a fingerprint without looking shiny.

Butter that is too warm turns greasy, separates and never sets cleanly. The fix: soften butter to 65 to 68°F (18 to 20°C). It should hold a fingerprint without looking shiny.

runs: The candle wasn't chilled long enough.
A candle that feels firm on the outside can still be soft in the center. The fix: honest chilling times, and a simple skewer test before you unmold.

runs: There was too much mix-in, or the wrong kind.
Wet ingredients like honey, sauces and fresh fruit make butter weep and slump. Too much cheese or chopped herbs leaves too little fat to hold the shape. The fix: the
chart, and freeze-dried fruit, powders and reductions in place of anything watery.

runs: The wick was wrong, or it touched the mix-ins.

Craft wicks are often waxed or metal-cored, and a wick surrounded by herbs, cheese or sugar will sputter, smoke and burn unevenly. The fix: untreated 100% cotton wicks, primed in clarified butter, and the
method for any candle with chunky mix-ins.

runs: Fresh herbs make the prettiest candles in the book: flecks of green suspended in gold. They also make the most fragrant ones, because the gentle heat of the pool releases their oils as you dip. runs: Nearly every food culture has a way of flavoring fat: North African spice pastes, Indian tempered ghee, Korean chili paste, Ethiopian spiced butter. This chapter takes those flavors and turns them into candles. Many are bolder and spicier than the rest of the book, so set them out with plenty of bread and a cooling dip, and let your guests travel the world from the table.

items.title: Tadka Ghee Candle
items.meta: Makes 1 standard candle · Serves 6 to 8  ·  Poured  ·  Active 25 minutes  ·  Chill 3 hours  ·  Burn about 45 to 60 minutes   V · GF · NF
items.image_brief: A clear golden-amber ghee candle, lit, on a brass thali plate with warm naan, a small bowl of dal and scattered curry leaves and spices; warm Indian kitchen styling.

runs: Tadka is the Indian technique of sizzling spices in hot ghee to release their flavor. Here the spiced ghee is strained and poured into a beautiful amber candle that smells incredible as it burns.
intro.html: Tadka is the Indian technique of sizzling spices in hot ghee to release their flavor. Here the spiced ghee is strained and poured into a beautiful amber candle that smells incredible as it burns.

runs: Heat ¼ cup (50 g) of the ghee in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the cumin and mustard seeds; when they begin to pop, after about 30 seconds, add the curry leaves and chilies and sizzle for 15 seconds more.

runs: Sweet edible candles are a delightful surprise at brunch, at afternoon tea or as dessert. Think of them as warm, melting sweet butter to dip brioche, waffles, fruit and cookies into. Two techniques make them work: powdered sugar instead of granulated (so the candle is silky, never gritty), and freeze-dried fruit ground to a powder (so you get bright fruit flavor and color with no water at all). Sugar caramelizes quickly near a flame, so every sweet candle uses the Clean-Burn Core.

runs: Margot Ellery is a home cook and dinner-party host who believes the best part of any gathering is the moment everyone reaches for the same loaf. Holiday tables, birthday spreads and last-minute dinners with friends taught her that guests remember one thing above all: the dish that made them stop and stare. Edible candles became that dish, but her first attempts slumped, cracked and smoked. So she did what home cooks do: she tested, adjusted and wrote everything down.
is the result, with every recipe written to work the first time.
